pharm: Biologically active, reduced form of folate (calcium salt of L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate) that does not require enzymatic conversion and is directly usable in one-carbon metabolism.
quick: Typically 7.5-15 mg once daily as a medical food/supplement (per product); supplemental folate varies by indication
May be taken with or without food; with food may improve tolerability
Folate is important in pregnancy (neural tube defect prevention); use product per clinician advice
Folate is compatible and often recommended during lactation
No specific adjustment; generally well tolerated
Chronic alcohol use impairs folate status; alcohol may reduce benefit
Clinical response; assess vitamin B12 to avoid masking deficiency
summary: L-Methylfolate calcium is the calcium salt of L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate (L-5-MTHF), the biologically active, predominant circulating form of folate. Unlike folic acid, it does not require reduction by methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), so it is directly available for one-carbon metabolism - including remethylation of homocysteine to methionine and production of the neurotransmitter precursors (it supports synthesis of tetrahydrobiopterin and monoamine neurotransmitters). It is marketed as a prescription medical food or dietary supplement, commonly to address suboptimal folate status, hyperhomocysteinemia, in patients with MTHFR polymorphisms, and as adjunctive support in certain depressive states. Doses commonly range from 7.5 to 15 mg daily depending on the product and intended use. IMPORTANT: it is not an FDA-approved drug; it is regulated as a medical food/dietary supplement, and high-dose folate can mask vitamin B12 deficiency.
indications: To provide bioavailable folate in individuals with suboptimal folate status or impaired folic acid metabolism (e.g., MTHFR variants)
Adjunctive nutritional support in distinct nutritional requirements such as hyperhomocysteinemia
Adjunctive use in major depressive disorder as a medical food (per product labeling)
Nutritional folate support in pregnancy and other states of increased folate demand (per clinician guidance)

dosage.d: Commonly 7.5 mg or 15 mg once daily (product dependent)
Commonly 15 mg once daily per product labeling
Lower amounts (e.g., 1 mg or less of L-methylfolate) in multivitamin/prenatal products

admin: Take orally once daily, with or without food
Use under the supervision of a physician when used as a prescription medical food
Continue B12 assessment, as folate can mask the hematologic signs of B12 deficiency
Store at room temperature, away from moisture and light
moa: Folate is essential for one-carbon transfer reactions. Dietary folic acid must be reduced and methylated by the enzyme methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) to L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate (L-5-MTHF) before it can be used. L-Methylfolate calcium supplies L-5-MTHF directly, bypassing the MTHFR step that is impaired in common genetic polymorphisms. L-5-MTHF is the methyl donor that converts homocysteine to methionine (via methionine synthase, regenerating tetrahydrofolate and requiring vitamin B12), supporting S-adenosylmethionine production and downstream methylation reactions, including those involved in monoamine neurotransmitter and tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to L-methylfolate or any product component
relative: Untreated/undiagnosed vitamin B12 deficiency (folate can mask hematologic signs while neurologic damage progresses)
Concurrent use of folate antagonists (efficacy/interaction considerations)
monitor: Vitamin B12 status before and during folate supplementation
Clinical response to the intended indication

preg: Adequate folate intake is important before and during pregnancy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects; L-methylfolate provides active folate and is used in some prenatal products. Use during pregnancy according to clinician guidance and product labeling; folate is generally considered beneficial in pregnancy.
lact: Folate is a normal component of breast milk and adequate maternal folate supports lactation; L-methylfolate supplementation is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is required for renal impairment; L-methylfolate is generally well tolerated. Excess water-soluble folate is renally excreted.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is required for hepatic impairment.

major: Methotrexate and other dihydrofolate-reductase inhibitors (e.g., pyrimethamine, trimethoprim) - folate may interact with antifolate therapy; coordinate with the prescriber
Capecitabine/fluorouracil - folate status can modify toxicity/efficacy
moderate: Antiepileptics (phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, valproate) - folate may lower their levels and they may lower folate; monitor seizure control
minor: Vitamin B12 - works together in homocysteine remethylation; ensure adequate B12
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; a balanced diet supports overall folate status.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use impairs folate absorption and metabolism, reducing benefit.
interactions.diagnostics: High folate intake can normalize the megaloblastic blood picture and mask vitamin B12 deficiency - check B12 to avoid missing it.

serious: Masking of vitamin B12 deficiency leading to unrecognized neurologic damage
rare: Skin rash, pruritus, or other hypersensitivity manifestations
Irritability or sleep disturbance (reported with high-dose active folate)

monitoring: Vitamin B12 level before starting and periodically to avoid masking deficiency
Clinical response to the intended use (e.g., mood, homocysteine)
Seizure control if used with antiepileptic drugs
counsel: This is an active form of folate (a B vitamin) and can be taken with or without food
Tell your doctor about all your medicines, especially seizure medicines, methotrexate, or sulfasalazine
Your doctor may check your vitamin B12 level, because folate can hide a B12 deficiency
If used in pregnancy, take it as directed - adequate folate helps protect the developing baby
Report any rash, itching, or signs of an allergic reaction
pk: Rapidly absorbed and incorporated into folate metabolism over hours to days
Plasma L-5-MTHF rises within a few hours of dosing
Folate stores turn over slowly; tissue effects persist beyond plasma levels
Store at room temperature (20-25 C); protect from moisture and light
pearls: NOT an FDA-approved drug - regulated/marketed as a prescription medical food or dietary supplement; this record is based on product labeling and nutrition references rather than an FDA drug label
Provides the active L-5-MTHF directly, bypassing the MTHFR conversion impaired by common genetic polymorphisms
High-dose folate can mask the megaloblastic anemia of vitamin B12 deficiency while neurologic damage continues - check B12
Works with vitamin B12 to remethylate homocysteine; useful in hyperhomocysteinemia and as adjunct in some depressive states
Coordinate with prescribers when patients are on antifolate drugs (methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine) or antiepileptics
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual once-daily schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Folate is water-soluble with a wide safety margin, and excess is generally excreted in the urine; acute toxicity from overdose is uncommon. Very high intakes may cause gastrointestinal upset, sleep disturbance, or irritability and can mask vitamin B12 deficiency. Provide supportive care if symptomatic and reassess vitamin B12 status.
